description:
Section B — Side-Channel Hygiene.

Two call sites in crate-jmap-base-client/src/blob.rs compare cryptographic-output hex strings with plain != operator on String:

1) blob.rs:301 (upload_blob) — `if local_sha256 != server_sha256.as_str()`
2) blob.rs:397 (download_blob) — `if actual != expected_lower`

Both compare 64-character hex strings. PartialEq on String compares byte-by-byte with early-exit on the first mismatch. A precise attacker timing the round-trip could in principle learn the longest matching prefix and reduce the digest-guess search space — for a 256-bit value this is academic in any practical setting, but the discipline against timing-side-channel comparisons on cryptographic outputs is standard.

# Why this is P3, not P2

The values being compared are HASHES of (mostly) public bytes, not MACs / authentication tags / password hashes. Discovering the digest of a blob the attacker can also download themselves gains them nothing. The standard 'compare MACs with constant-time' rule is targeting cases where:

- The expected value is a secret the attacker is trying to forge (HMAC tag)
- The actual value is derived from attacker-controlled input (HMAC over an attacker-supplied message)

Neither applies here. SHA-256 of blob bytes is not a secret. The integrity check just notices in-transit corruption.

That said:

- The download_blob case takes expected_sha256 from the caller. If the caller obtained that digest from a private channel (separate signed manifest, end-to-end attestation), then a timing attack on the digest comparison COULD leak partial information about the expected digest to a remote attacker. Implausible threat model for JMAP today, but the field exists.

- The workspace already takes the discipline of explicit constant-time compare on credentials (BearerAuth's HeaderValue::from_str validation is single-shot, not byte-loop). The discipline-creep argument says: adopt the same posture for all cryptographic-output comparisons.

# What goes wrong (timing leak — bounded)

Worst case, an attacker who can repeatedly trigger upload_blob/download_blob on the same expected digest and time the call learns one byte at a time which prefix of the expected digest matches. For a 256-bit digest this is bounded by 32 successful + 16 average failed comparisons per byte — measurable on a LAN, much harder over WAN. Realistically: not exploitable in JMAP threat models.

# Suggested fix

Use subtle::ConstantTimeEq from the subtle crate (already in the workspace tree via sha2's deps):

```rust
use subtle::ConstantTimeEq;

if local_sha256.as_bytes().ct_eq(server_sha256.as_str().as_bytes()).unwrap_u8() == 0 {
    // mismatch
}
```

The hex-string comparison is byte-stable (both sides are canonical lowercase 64-hex), so ct_eq is correct. Document the rationale inline.

Alternative: lift the comparison into a small helper `fn hex_digest_eq(a: &str, b: &str) -> bool` with the ct_eq inside; reuse the helper at both call sites. That also makes the call-site code easier to scan for reviewers.

# Test discipline

Constant-time compare resists differential timing tests via cycle-count probes. The standard discipline is to assert behavioral equality vs ==, not to assert timing — a unit test cannot validate side-channel resistance, only the compiler/CPU pipeline can. The fix is a one-line semantic change with the doc-comment carrying the discipline argument.

# References

- subtle crate documentation, ConstantTimeEq trait
- RustCrypto's design guidance: constant-time compares on all crypto-output equality checks even when the field is public, for discipline propagation
title: SHA-256 hex digest equality uses String ==, not constant-time compare (defense-in-depth, low real impact)
